findings.summary: The last_modified check can't tell an updated timestamp from the creation time, because POST and PATCH run in the same second
findings.failure_scenario: Say a partial fix sets last_modified_by in OIDCClientStore.update but drops the line `oidc_client.last_modified = datetime_to_db(now)`, and keeps the whole-second truncation in create(). This is exactly the reported bug: last_modified still holds the creation time. The POST at line 124 and the PATCH at line 142 almost always land in the same wall-clock second, so the stored last_modified (= created, truncated) equals `before` (truncated). `last_modified >= before` and `>= created` both pass, and GET/list agree with it. test_patch_last_modified_not_before_send_time passes, and so does every other test. On base this test fails only on the fractional-second regex, not on the timestamp behaviour. The fixture has to make the update observable: give the client a `created`/`last_modified` well in the past before the PATCH, then assert that last_modified moved.

findings.summary: The check that created is unchanged by a PATCH has the same same-second blind spot
findings.failure_scenario: Suppose update() wrongly sets `oidc_client.created = datetime_to_db(now)`. With the truncation from create(), the reset value equals the original created whenever POST and PATCH share a second. The comparisons at lines 85, 103, 154, 168, 211 and 288 all still pass, so nothing checks the criterion 'created is the same before and after a PATCH'. A client whose created is clearly in the past would expose it.

findings.summary: last_modified has a lower bound but no upper bound, so a wrong future timestamp passes
findings.failure_scenario: Suppose update() records a time hours ahead, for example naive `datetime.now()` local time treated as UTC on a host east of UTC, or a stray timedelta. `last_modified >= before` and `>= created` still hold. The contract says last_modified is the time of that update, and the existing api_oidc_test checks `start <= created <= now`. Here no `after = datetime.now(tz=UTC)` is taken after the PATCH and asserted as `last_modified <= after`.

findings.summary: The whole-second regex also accepts `+00:00`, but the contract's format is the `Z` form
findings.failure_scenario: The contract gives `2026-10-14T15:44:22Z` as the serialised form. If a serializer change made the API emit `2026-10-14T15:44:22+00:00`, the format would change for API clients and assert_whole_seconds would still pass.

findings.summary: The refused-PATCH test leaves out the cookie-without-CSRF 403 case that the contract lists
findings.failure_scenario: The contract says a cookie without its X-CSRF-Token gives 403 and the client stays unchanged afterwards. The test covers 401, token-403, 422 and 404, but never sends a session-cookie PATCH without the CSRF header. A regression that applied the update (or the audit fields) before the CSRF check rejects the request would go unnoticed here. test_csrf_required in api_oidc_test.py only checks the status code.

findings.summary: test_patch_by_creator_keeps_creator_as_modifier and test_refused_patch_leaves_client_unchanged both pass on the base commit
findings.failure_scenario: On 9b61018, update() never touches last_modified_by, so it stays 'admin-a' and the refused PATCHes change nothing. Both tests pass on the pre-fix code, which goes against the strategy rule that a test must fail on the code before the change. They are acceptable as regression guards for criteria the ticket says don't change, but this should be written down as a deliberate choice.
